 Judgment

This is petition filed under Section 166 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, seeking compensation of Rs.75,00,000/- from the respondents on account of death of D.M. Ramanjinappa, who is husband of petitioner No.1, father of petitioners No.2 to 4 and son of petitioners No.5, in a road traffic accident.

(Earlier this petition was filed by the deceased petitioner namely D.M. Ramanjinappa under Section 166 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1989, seeking compensation of Rs.50,00,000/- from the respondents, for the grievous injuries sustained by him in a road traffic accident.

During the course of trial, the petitioner died and his legal heirs came on record and have claimed compensation from the respondents for the death of the deceased petitioner)
2.

The brief facts of the case are as follows:
On 28-07-2019 at about 12:40 p.m., the deceased D.M. Ramanjinappa was riding his motorcycle bearing No.KA-51-V- 3816 on Hosakote-Chintamani Road, carefully and cautiously.

When he reached near Siddhartha Nagar Bridge, all of a sudden a tipper lorry bearing No.KA-53-D-5913, being driven by its driver in high speed, rash and negligent manner, neglecting all the rules and regulations, came from behind and dashed to the motorcycle of deceased.
Due to said impact, the deceased fell down and sustained grievous injuries to his face, head, right hand and other parts of the body.

The accident occurred due to the negligence on the part of the petitioner/deceased being rider of motorcycle without having proper look out vehicular movements of the road and without noticing on coming vehicles and was riding the motorcycle recklessly and carelessly and caused the accident.

Later he was shifted to Manipal Hospital,
Bengaluru for better treatment, wherein he has taken treatment as an inpatient from 28-07-2019 to 17-08-2019.

On 17-08-2019, he got admitted at Silicon City Hospital as post craniectomy status with bone flap infection in abdominal wall done on 03-10-2019 left FTP mesh cranioplasty done under GA and discharged.

On 30-09-2021 the deceased brought to emergency department with history of not responding since one hour.

Further it is contended that, before accident the deceased was working as an agriculturist and was earning Rs.20,000/- per month.
He was contributing his entire earnings to his family.
Due to untimely death of a sole bread earner, the petitioners are struggling for their livelihood.
11. In order to prove their case, the petitioner No.1 has got examined herself as P.W.1 by filing examination-in-chief affidavit, wherein she has reiterated the averments made in the petition.
Further, in support of her oral evidence, the petitioner No.1 has got marked total 15 documents as Ex.P.1 to 15.

Out of the said documents, Ex.P.1 is copy of F.I.R., Ex.P.2 is copy of first information statement, Ex.P.3 is copy of spot mahazar, Ex.P.4 is copy of Motor Vehicle Accident report, Ex.P.5 is copy of wound certificate, Ex.P.6 is copy of charge-sheet, Ex.P.7 are discharge summaries (total 3),
Ex.P.8 is copy of death summary, Ex.P.9 are photographs (total 6) with one CD, Ex.P.10 are medical bills (total 84), Ex.P.11 are medical prescriptions (total 73) and Ex.P.12 to 15 are case-sheets (total 4).
12. At the outset, it is pertinent to note that, the date, time and place of accident, involvement of offending vehicle, issuance of insurance policy and its validity are not in dispute.

Further, though the respondent No.1 and 2 have specifically denied the above facts in their written statement, they have not produced any rebuttal evidence to disprove the oral and documentary evidence placed on record by the petitioners.
Further, the respondent No.1 and 2 have not even stepped into the witness box to depose the contentions in their written statement on oath.

There is absolutely no oral or documentary evidence placed on record by the respondents, to show that, the alleged accident has occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the deceased and not due to rash and negligent driving of the driver of the Tipper lorry.

The P.W.1 has unequivocally denied the suggestion made to her by the learned counsel for respondent No.1 that, the offending lorry bearing Reg. No.KA-53-D-5913 is not at all involved in the alleged accident and the same has been caused by some unknown vehicle.

Further, she has denied the suggestion that, her husband while driving his motorcycle in high speed Ramanjinappa vs Royal Sun All Ins Co Ltd on 7 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/166360776/

13. On meticulously going through the police documents marked as Ex.P.1 to 6, prima-facia it reveals that, on 28-07- 2019 at about 12:40 p.m., when the deceased D.M. Ramanjinappa was riding his motorcycle bearing No.KA-51- V-3816 on Hosakote-Chintamani Road, near Siddhartha Nagar Bridge, all of a sudden the driver of the offending tipper lorry bearing No.KA-53-D-5913 drove the same in rash and negligent manner, in high speed, came from behind and dashed to the motorcycle of deceased.

Due to the impact, the deceased fell down and sustained grievous injuries to his face,
head, right hand and other parts of the body.

On the other hand, except the self serving statements of the respondent No.1 & 2, there is absolutely no other oral and documentary evidence placed on record by the respondents to rebut the final report of the investigation officer and other police documents produced by the petitioners, particularly with respect to date, time and place of accident,
rash and negligent driving of the driver of offending lorry and injuries sustained by the deceased in the said accident.
14. The oral evidence of P.W.1 is fully corroborated with the documentary evidence marked as Ex.P.1 to 15.
Though, the learned counsel for respondents No.1 and 2 have cross- examined P.W.1 in length

,
nothing worth has been elicited from her mouth which creates doubt on the veracity of her evidence.
15. The Ex.P.3 spot mahazer clearly speaks that, the said accident has taken place towards extreme left side of 30 feet width Hoskote-Chintamani main road, near Siddhartha Nagar Bridge.
Further it reveals that, there was sufficient space towards right side of the place of accident, to avoid the accident by the driver of offending lorry.
There is absolutely no evidence on record to show that, at the time of accident the deceased was riding his motorcycle in rash and negligent manner.

In such circumstances, if really as contended by the respondents, there was no rash and negligent driving on the part of driver of offending lorry and he was driving his vehicle in moderate speed, definitely he would have avoided the said accident.
16. Further it is pertinent to note, as per Ex.P.4 Motor Vehicle Accident Report, the accident had not occurred due to any mechanical defects in the vehicles involved in the accident.

When the accident was not occurred due to the any mechanical defects in the offending vehicle and there was no negligence on the part of motorcycle rider, then in the present facts and circumstances of the case it can be presumed that, the said accident had occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the driver of offending vehicle.

Further, the investigation officer has clearly stated in the final report, marked as Ex.P.6, that, the alleged accident has occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the driver of the offending vehicle bearing Reg. No. KA-53-D-5913.

There is absolutely no rebuttal evidence led by the respondents to disprove the case of the petitioners and even nothing is elicited in the cross-examination of P.W.1 to show that, the alleged accident has occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the deceased and there is no negligence on the part of the driver of tipper lorry bearing Reg. No. KA-53-D- 5913.

18.

The above medical records clearly goes to show that, since from the date of accident the deceased petitioner was suffering from breathing and decreased neurological response, on account of severe head injury and on other vital parts of the deceased petitioner.
Further, the deceased petitioner was under continuous treatment for the above injuries.

No doubt, as per the above medical records there are some intervals between the discharge date from one hospital and re-admitting date in another hospital for further treatment and there is long gap in between the date of accident and the date of death.

For the mere reason that, there were some intervals between the discharge date from one hospital and re-admitting date in another hospital for further treatment and there is long gap in between the date of accident and the date of death, it cannot be held that, there is no nexus in between the injuries suffered by the deceased petitioner in the accident and cause of his death.

Further, the above medical records clearly reveals that, since from the date of accident the health of the deceased petitioner was slowly deteriorating and finally he has succumbed to above injuries on 30-09-2021, at Silicon City Hospital, Bengaluru.
On the other hand, there is nothing on record to show that, deceased Ramanjinappa has died due to some other cause or disease.

Further, though the respondents are specifically contended that, there is no nexus between the injuries suffered in the accident and the death of deceased petitioner, they have not produced any evidence to show that,
the deceased petitioner has died due to any other cause or disease.
There is absolutely no material on record to disbelieve the above medical records placed on record by the petitioners.

19. Further, it is well settled principle of law that, in a case relating to the Motor Accident Claims,
the claimants are not required to prove the case as required to be done in a criminal trial.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Parameshwari V/s Amir Chand and others, reported in (2011)
SCC 635, has clearly held that, "in a road accident claim cases the strict principle of proof as in a criminal case are not required."

22. Issue No.2:

While answering above issue, for the reasons stated therein, this Court has already held that, the petitioners have successfully proved through cogent and corroborative evidence that,
the alleged accident has caused due to rash and negligent driving of the driver of offending Tipper lorry bearing Reg. No. KA-53-D-5913 and the deceased Ramanjinappa has succumbed to the grievous injuries sustained in the said accident.

Now the petitioners are required to establish that,
they are the legal representatives of the deceased.
No doubt the petitioners are not tendered and got marked any documents to show that they are the legal heirs of deceased Ramanjinappa.

But, the petitioners in support of their interim application filed under Order XXII Rule 3 & 4 CPC have produced the copies of their respective Aadhar cards, death certificate of Ramanjinappa and the genealogy certificate issued by the Deputy Tahsildar, Jadigenahalli Hobli, Hoskote Taluk.

Further,
relying on the said documents this court has already allowed the above interim application, holding that the petitioners are the legal heirs of the deceased Ramanjinappa and they have been permitted to come on record.
On the other hand, the respondents have not disputed the relationship of petitioners with the deceased Ramanjinappa.
Further, nothing contrary with respect to same has been elicited in the cross-examination of PW1.
In such circumstances, there is no impediment to believe the above documents produced by the petitioners and hold that, the petitioners are the legal representatives of deceased Ramanjinappa.

23. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in the case of National Insurance Co. V/s Birender, reported in (2020) 11 SCC 356, has clearly held that, "12. The legal representatives of the deceased could move application for compensation by virtue of clause (c) of Section 166(1).

sentences.text: The major married son who is also earning and not fully dependant on the deceased, would be still covered by the expression "legal representative" of the deceased.
This Court in Manjuri Bera (supra) had expounded that liability to pay compensation under the Act does not cease because of absence of dependency of the concerned legal representative.
Notably, the expression "legal representative" has not been defined in the Act.
10. The Tribunal has a duty to make an award, determine the amount of compensation which is just and proper and specify the person or persons to whom such compensation would be paid.
The latter part relates to the entitlement of compensation by a person who claims for the same.

sentences.text: According to Section 2(11) CPC, "legal representative" means a person who in law represents the Tractor and Trally bearing No.AP-03-AN-8690 & AP-03-AN-8712 estate of a deceased person, and includes any person who intermeddles with the estate of the deceased and where a party sues or is sued in a representative character the person on whom the estate devolves on the death of the party so suing or sued.

Almost in similar terms is the definition of legal representative under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 i.e. under Section 2(1)(g).
12.

As observed by this Court in Custodian of Branches of BANCO National Ultramarino vs. Nalini Bai Naique [1989 Supp (2) SCC 275, the definition contained in Section 2(11) CPC is inclusive in character and its scope is wide, it is not confined to legal heirs only.

entities.text: Custodian of Branches of BANCO National Ultramarino vs. Nalini Bai Naique [1989 Supp (2) SCC 275
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Instead it stipulates that, a person who may or may not be legal heir competent to inherit the property of the deceased can represent the estate of the deceased person.
It includes heirs as well as persons who represent the estate even without title either as executors or administrators in possession of the estate of the deceased.
All such persons would be covered by the expression "legal representative".

As observed in Gujarat SRTC vs. Ramanbhai Prabhatbhai [(1987) 3 SCC 234 a legal representative is one who suffers on account of death of a person due to a motor vehicle accident and need not necessarily be a wife, husband, parent and child.

sentences.text: 13. In Manjuri Bera (supra), in paragraph 15 of the said decision, while adverting to the provisions of Section 140 of the Act, the Court observed that even if there is no loss of dependency, the claimant, if he was a legal representative, will be entitled to compensation.
In the concurring judgment of Justice S. H. Kapadia, as His Lordship then was, it is observed that there is distinction between "right to apply for compensation" and "entitlement to compensation".
The compensation constitutes part of the estate of the deceased.
As a result, the legal representative of the deceased would inherit the estate.
Indeed, in that case, the Court was dealing with the case of a married daughter of the deceased and the efficacy of Section 140 of the Act.
Nevertheless, the principle underlying the exposition in this decision would clearly (claimants) even though they are major sons of the deceased and also earning.
14. It is thus settled by now that the legal representatives of the deceased have a right to apply for compensation.

Having said that, it must necessarily follow that even the major married and earning sons of the deceased being legal representatives have a right to apply for compensation and it would be the bounden duty of the Tribunal to consider the application irrespective of the fact whether the concerned legal representative was fully dependent on the deceased and not to limit the claim towards conventional heads only."

24. According to the ratio laid down in above decision, the legal representatives though not fully dependent on the deceased are entitled to claim compensation under all the heads i.e., under both conventional and non-conventional heads.

In order to determine the compensation, the age,
avocation, income, dependency, future prospects of the deceased and other conventional heads are to be ascertained.
25. The compensation towards loss of dependency:

Further, they have stated that,
they were depending upon the deceased.
Hence, they are entitled to compensation under the head of loss of dependency.
In order to calculate the loss of dependency, the first step is to determine the age and income of the deceased.
i) Age and income of the deceased :
The petitioners have averred that, the age of deceased as on the date of accident was 47 years.
Whereas, in the petition the age of the deceased petitioner as on the date of filing of the petition is mentioned as 45 years.
But, in Ex.P.8 death summary, the age of the deceased petitioner as on the date of death is mentioned as 48 years.
In view of medical records, the age of the deceased petitioner as on the date of death is considered as 48 years.
The petitioners have stated that, as on the date of death the deceased was hale and healthy and was working as an agriculturist and was earning a sum of Rs.20,000/- per month.
But, the petitioners have not produced any document to show the deceased Ramanjinappa was working as an agriculturist and he was earning Rs.20,000/- per month.

In such circumstances, there is no other option before this Court, except to consider the notional income as income of the deceased as per the guidelines of the Karnataka State Legal Services Authority.

The Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in the cases of, G. T. Basavaraj V/s Niranjan and another, in MFA No.7781/2016, judgment dated 11-08-2022, Ramanna and another V/s Y. B. Mahesh and another in MFA No.140/2017, judgment dated 16-01-2020 and New India Assurance Co. Ltd., V/s Anusaya and others in MFA No.101195/2014, judgment dated 05-01-2023, has clearly held that,

No doubt, as per the above medical records there are some intervals between the discharge date from one hospital and re-admitting date in another hospital for further treatment and there is long gap in between the date of accident and the date of death.
For the mere reason that, there were some intervals between the discharge date from one hospital and re-admitting date in another hospital for further treatment and there is long gap in between the date of accident and the date of death, it cannot be held that, there is no nexus in between the injuries suffered by the deceased petitioner in the accident and cause of his death.
Further, though the respondents are specifically contended that, there is no nexus between the injuries suffered in the accident and the death of deceased petitioner, they have not produced any evidence to show that,
the deceased petitioner has died due to any other cause or disease.
19. Further, it is well settled principle of law that, in a case relating to the Motor Accident Claims,
the claimants are not required to prove the case as required to be done in a criminal trial.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Parameshwari V/s Amir Chand and others, reported in (2011)
SCC 635, has clearly held that, "in a road accident claim cases the strict principle of proof as in a criminal case are not required."

Almost in similar terms is the definition of legal representative under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 i.e. under Section 2(1)(g).

As observed by this Court in Custodian of Branches of BANCO National Ultramarino vs. Nalini Bai Naique [1989 Supp (2) SCC 275, the definition contained in Section 2(11) CPC is inclusive in character and its scope is wide, it is not confined to legal heirs only.
Instead it stipulates that, a person who may or may not be legal heir competent to inherit the property of the deceased can represent the estate of the deceased person.
It includes heirs as well as persons who represent the estate even without title either as executors or administrators in possession of the estate of the deceased.
All such persons would be covered by the expression "legal representative".
As observed in Gujarat SRTC vs. Ramanbhai Prabhatbhai [(1987) 3 SCC 234 a legal representative is one who suffers on account of death of a person due to a motor vehicle accident and need not necessarily be a wife, husband, parent and child.
